logline: A terminally ill woman accidentally summons the personification of doom with a drunken wish, then signs a hundred-day contract with him - gambling her life against the world's annihilation in a romance built on borrowed time.

renewal.note: Single-season 16-episode run concluded June 29, 2021. Pre-sold to 150 countries; no sequel produced.

bollymeter.basis: Park Bo-young and Seo In-guk's chemistry is the engine - critics and audiences agreed it overcame a screenplay that leaned on cliches; IMDb settled at 7.8 and the show ranked on NME's best K-dramas of 2021 list.

seasons.review_body: Doom at Your Service aired on tvN from May to June 2021, averaging 3.027 percent nationwide cable ratings with a peak of 4.422 percent in episode two. The show was pre-sold to 150 countries and made available on Viki, Viu, and iQIYI, reflecting substantial international commercial positioning ahead of broadcast. NME placed it tenth on their best K-dramas of 2021 list. Critical conversation centred almost entirely on the lead pairing: Seo In-guk as a supernatural entity who delivers annihilation with deadpan menace, and Park Bo-young as a woman who refuses to be intimidated by her own death sentence. Detractors noted the screenplay relied on cliches and left emotional threads at a superficial level; defenders argued the leads transcended the writing. IMDb settled at 7.8, a solid placement for the genre.

episode_reviews.title: Episode 1
episode_reviews.review_body: Doom at Your Service's premiere establishes its central contract with unusual directness: Tak Dong-kyung (Park Bo-young), terminally ill and drunk, issues a careless curse that summons Myeolmang (Seo In-guk) - a being who embodies doom and who offers a bargain. The episode's quality is in making Dong-kyung's response to this situation immediately characterise her: she does not behave like a victim, she negotiates. Writer Im Me-ah-ri positions the supernatural romance with the tone of dark comedy and genuine pathos held simultaneously, which separates the premiere from generic entries in the format. Seo In-guk's entrance as Myeolmang was calibrated for maximum unsettling charm - a supernatural entity played with the specific quality of someone who has never needed to perform normality - and the premiere demonstrates the series' strongest decision: casting two actors whose registers work together without cancelling each other out.
episode_reviews.spoiler_free: The premiere establishes the central contract - a dying woman summons doom and then refuses to behave like a victim - in a way that immediately separates the show from generic supernatural romance. Seo In-guk's entrance is calibrated for maximum unsettling charm and it works. The tone balances dark comedy and genuine pathos without collapsing either.
episode_reviews.the_moment: Dong-kyung's drunken curse lands - and doom materialises not as a monster but as a man with unreadable eyes.

episode_reviews.title: Episode 16
episode_reviews.review_body: Doom at Your Service's finale resolves the supernatural contract in a way that divided audience reactions cleanly: one reading finds the ending earned by sixteen episodes of specific character work; the other finds the resolution too convenient given the genuinely high stakes the series had maintained. The critical consensus on the finale was that the show's ambition exceeded its ability to honour it at the conclusion - the mythology frays slightly under the pressure of resolution, and the choices made about Myeolmang's fate required narrative manoeuvres that the series' logic had not fully prepared. What the finale does sustain is the performances: Park Bo-young and Seo In-guk remain committed to the emotional register they had maintained across sixteen episodes, and the individual character beats of the finale close land with more force than the mythology's resolution. The moment Myeolmang's choice becomes irrevocable was identified by viewers as the scene that reframed the entire hundred-day premise.
episode_reviews.spoiler_free: The finale resolves the supernatural contract in a way that divides reactions: one group finds the ending earned, while another feels the resolution is too convenient given sixteen episodes of genuinely high stakes. The lead performances stay committed to the end, and the emotional close lands on individual character beats even when the mythology frays.
episode_reviews.the_moment: The moment Myeolmang's choice becomes irrevocable - a scene that reframes the entire hundred-day premise.
